title: The Experience, Captured
objective: Experience the arts, review a craft choice and its effect, then share your view and record whom, how and where the evidence is saved.

blocks.text: BUILD · Art · Week 5. Trinity Arts Award Bronze. The Experience, Captured.
Objective: Experience the arts, review a craft choice and its effect, then share your view and record whom, how and where the evidence is saved.
Success evidence: a record of the experience, your view of its quality and effect, and a located record of sharing that view with another person.

Everything you capture comes from the work in front of you, or from a card in the approved pack. You write about the work: colour, scale, material, sound. You are never asked about your home, your family, your body, how you look or what you believe. Nobody in this room is asked what they believe. Identity here means what you as a maker keep choosing, read off artwork and never off a life.

Nothing is booked. No event and no place is named in this deck. We may go to them. They may come to us. We may meet live on a screen. An online exhibition counts as well. The frame works the same under all three.
40 minutes. Paper and a pencil are all you need to capture.

This deck evidences Bronze Part B, Explore the arts as an audience member. The register says Part B requires attending at least one arts event or experience, reflecting on quality and creative impact, and views shared with at least one other person, evidenced. The register also notes that an online exhibition is legitimate. Nothing is booked: the event comes from EVENT_SLOT, which is UNCONFIRMED, and no venue, organisation, practitioner or date is named anywhere in this deck. It runs unchanged under R1 pupils visit, R2 they come in, and R3 a live remote exchange. Where the experience has not yet run, a card from the approved pack stands in and the rows are labelled preparation, because the slots file counts desk research, archive and video as preparation only. Bronze attempted rule, in the register's words: ONE Attempted allowed overall. Any Not Attempted = Below Pass. The evidence file cap is 10 evidence files for the whole Bronze level, so today's frame sheet joins the Part B file rather than opening a new one. The three assessment areas are art form knowledge and understanding, creativity, and communication.

Delivery is through a validated centre; confirm local validation and an adviser trained at Bronze before assessment. Neither is asserted as completed here. Core, Extend and Challenge are support routes inside Bronze, not different awards. The prompts and sample quantities are teaching scaffolds, not extra assessment requirements. Scribe only the pupil’s own words. Store evidence by part; one cumulative file per part is a suggested four-file plan within the ten-file cap.

Read the current EVENT_SLOT from tools/artsaward/SLOTS.json before delivery. Reserve a genuine audience experience, including an online exhibition, then review and share in this sequence. Allow the event its real running time; this forty-minute lesson does not limit a longer event or claim all sixty Bronze hours. If the slot is still empty, use only the labelled preparation route and return to the actual experience and share later. An archive clip or desk card is preparation, not proof of attendance. The pupil must reflect on quality and creative impact, not just list details. Add pages to Part B; record the actual event, recipient, method and file plus page/slide/timecode after it happens.

stages.title: Arrival · retrieve
stages.data-ta1: Check EVENT_SLOT before the lesson. Announce whether this is the actual experience or preparation. Keep the route label visible; do not imply a booking.

blocks.text: Bring the frame back
Your frame has four boxes in each row.
They hold a moment, a craft choice, its effect and its audience.
Read the row you tried in the last lesson.
That row came from the pack. It is preparation.
Today an adult will tell you which route is ready.
We may go out, guests may come in, or we may meet live on screen.
An online exhibition can be the real arts experience too.
If no experience is ready, keep the word preparation on your work.
Never change that label to make a folder look full.
Put your blank frame and a pencil where you can reach them.

stages.title: Starter · create the need
stages.data-ta1: Draw six thin lines with a white gap as the practice example. Read both views yourself; do not cast a pupil as the weak reviewer.

blocks.text: A list is not yet a review
Listen to two practice views of a made-up line drawing.
The first says: there are six lines and a white space.
The second says: the thin lines leave a clear space, so my eye rests there.
Both views name things in the work.
Only the second links a choice to what it does.
A review gives your view, with a reason from the work.
You can like a work and still spot a weak choice.
You can dislike it and still explain a strong choice.
There is no right feeling to copy from the adult.
Which view gives a reader a reason they can check?
Point at first or second, then name the useful words.

stages.title: I Do · model
stages.data-ta1: Model with the drawing made in the starter. Point as you speak. Keep fact, judgement and effect separate; accept a different reason supported by the work.

blocks.text: Choice, quality, effect
Watch how I build a review of the practice drawing.
First I point at the narrow gap between two lines.
Next I name the choice: the lines are close together.
Then I judge its quality: the gap is clear all the way down.

blocks.title: From a moment to a shared review
blocks.caption: A reason connects your view to the work
blocks.alt: Boxes labelled NOTICE, JUDGE, EXPLAIN, SHARE. A reason connects your view to the work

blocks.text: That tells you how well the choice works.
Last I say its effect: my eye follows the gap down the page.
That tells you what the choice did for me.
I join those ideas with because.
The close lines guide my eye because the gap stays clear.
Quality does not mean that every mark must be neat.
A rough sound or torn edge can work well for its purpose.
I would judge that choice by what it helps the work do.
My view is an example. Do not copy it into your own review.
Your reason comes from the real work you see or hear.

stages.title: We Do · everyone commits
stages.data-ta1: Show all three notes at once. Give private thinking time, then let pupils point or read; check the link rather than demanding the model wording. The exact sorting lines are on this slide: project them and let pupils sort by number, or copy these lines onto cards. No separate pack is required for this sort.

blocks.text: Sort the three kinds of note
Read these three notes about the practice drawing.
The lines are close together.
The gap is clear from top to bottom.
My eye follows the gap down the page.
Point to the note that names a choice.
Now point to the note that judges how well it works.
Last, point to the note that names its effect.
Say which words helped you decide.
All three can fit in one short review.
If you only have an effect, look back for the choice that caused it.
If you only have a fact, ask what that fact did for you.

stages.title: I Do 2 · connect
stages.data-ta1: Demonstrate a short share and its locator. A staff note may record what happened; staff must not compose the pupil’s view.

blocks.text: Share the view, keep the proof
Writing a review and sharing it are two different steps.
A page in a closed folder has not reached an audience.
I can read my view to a member of staff.
I can show a peer my review and talk it through.

blocks.title: Two parts of the evidence
blocks.caption: Keep the review and its share together
blocks.alt: Boxes labelled REVIEW, SHARE RECORD. Keep the review and its share together

blocks.text: I can play my spoken review to a small group.
The person needs to receive my view, not just hold the paper.
Then I keep a record of who received it and how.
A short note or a sound clip can show that step.
Initials are one option, not a special rule of the award.
The file name alone may leave a reader searching.
Give the page, slide or time in the file as well.
For example: Bronze-B, page three, review shared with class staff.
Use the real file name and page for your own work.

stages.title: We Do 2 · lab
stages.data-ta1: Pair by agreed support needs and allow a staff audience. Do not insist on public performance. Keep this rehearsal separate from the actual Part B evidence.

blocks.text: Try the link before the experience
Look once more at the practice drawing.
Choose a line or a gap and point at it.
Say what works well or could work better.
Say what that choice does for your eye.
Use because to link your view to the part you chose.
An adult can write your exact words if you want.
Read the view to someone at your table.
Ask which part they pictured from your words.
If they pictured a different part, make your clue more clear.
Record whom you told and how you told them.
Label this practice. It is not the event review.
Keep the frame ready for the experience that comes next.

stages.title: Independent · evidence
stages.data-ta1: Give at least the first eight minutes to uninterrupted viewing/listening, extending beyond the lesson if the event needs it. Then support the pupil’s own review. Record only an experience that happened; do not fill absent evidence.

blocks.text: Experience, then give your view
Now take part as an audience member in the experience in use.
Look or listen first. Give the work time to unfold.
An adult will give you a quiet cue to make a note.
Choose one moment or one part that stayed with you.
Name a craft choice you saw or heard there.
It might be a colour, a shape, a beat or a material.
Describe how well that choice worked, with a reason.
Then say what effect it had on you as an audience member.
You may record a second moment if it helps you compare.
Build your short review from those notes, in your own words.
Check that your view points back to the actual work.
Do not use the made-up line drawing as event evidence.
If this lesson is preparation, keep that label and return to this step after the real experience.
Keep a note of the event or exhibition you actually experienced.
It can be added to your Part B file with your review.

items: Core · Use the prompt boxes and an adult scribe to record your own view of quality and effect. Share it and locate the evidence.
Extend · Write or record your review with a reason from the work. Share it, and record whom, how and its locator.
Challenge · As Extend, compare two craft choices and explain which affected your own ideas more.

stages.title: Exit · Audience and Influence
stages.data-ta1: Confirm the recipient actually received the review. Accept writing, faithful scribing or located audio/video. If the experience was only rehearsal, record a practice share and leave the genuine Part B evidence open.

blocks.text: Let your review reach someone
Choose a peer, a small group or a staff member.
Read your review to them, show it to them or play your clip.
Share what you thought of the quality and what effect it had.
Let the person ask which part led to your view.
You can keep your view when someone disagrees with it.
Record whom you shared with and how you shared it.
Keep the note or clip beside your review in the Part B file.
Write the actual file name and page, slide or timecode.
Check that someone else can find both the review and the share.
Choose one craft choice from the experience to test in your own art.
Say why that choice caught your interest.

print.intro: Keep your own view. Label rehearsal as preparation. After the real experience, record the review and the share.
focusRows: The experience actually seen or heard, through the route in use.
Your view of quality and creative impact, grounded in the work.
Who received the review, how, and the evidence locator.
tiers: Use the prompt boxes and an adult scribe to record your own view of quality and effect. Share it and locate the evidence.
Write or record your review with a reason from the work. Share it, and record whom, how and its locator.
As Extend, compare two craft choices and explain which affected your own ideas more.
checks: The record identifies an actual arts experience; rehearsal is clearly labelled preparation.
The pupil’s own review explains quality and creative impact with a reason from the work.
At least one other person received the review; whom and how are recorded.
The actual file name plus page, slide or timecode locates both the review and the sharing record.
